description: A worn device in a living room with the TV on. Cricket commentary and an advert are audible alongside a real conversation. Guards prompt rule 13 in both directions: broadcast audio must not become anyone's task, and the user's own statement ABOUT television must still be extracted. This is the documented #1 failure of the competition - Forbes on Bee: to-dos 'teased out of entertainment content that Bee has mistaken for things I said'.
transcript: That's a big shot over midwicket they will need to bring Bumrah back before the break Yeah turn it down a bit So listen I'll transfer you the rent tomorrow okay Fine Call now and get a second one absolutely free limited stock offer ends midnight What channel is this even Remind me to watch the final tomorrow I don't want to miss it again Also day after tomorrow I have to submit the hostel form

expected_items.quote: I'll transfer you the rent tomorrow
expected_items.note: A real commitment by a person in the room, spoken between two pieces of broadcast audio. If rule 13 is too aggressive this is the item it will swallow.

THE CRITICAL ASSERTION, and the reason rule 13 tests presence rather than topic. The subject is television, so a topic-based media rule suppresses it - but the USER said it, about their own evening, with a date. Rule 11 also applies: 'Remind me to' is folded into the thing to be remembered rather than becoming a date-less item of its own.

expected_items.quote: day after tomorrow I have to submit the hostel form
expected_items.note: An ordinary personal errand, included so the case fails if rule 13 depresses extraction generally rather than only on broadcast spans.

must_suppress_as_media: bring Bumrah back before the break
Call now and get a second one absolutely free
decision_note: The two must_suppress_as_media spans are the classic shapes: sports commentary phrased as a requirement ('they will need to bring Bumrah back'), and advertising phrased as an assignment ('Call now'). Both are grammatically perfect actionable items and belong to nobody, which is exactly why a topic-blind extractor files them. Asserting they appear in `dropped` with a media reason - rather than merely asserting they are absent from `items` - matters: absence would also be satisfied by the model simply ignoring that part of the transcript, which is luck, not suppression. If this case ever fails on item 2 while passing the suppression checks, rule 13 has become too broad and should be narrowed, not strengthened.
must_not_extract: anything spoken by the television - the advert or the commentary
a task belonging to a person who was not in the room
